{{For|a related alternating series of factorials|1 − 1 + 2 − 6 + 24 − 120 + ⋯}}
{{No footnotes|date=September 2021}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''alternating factorial''' is the [[absolute value]] of the [[alternating sum]] of the first ''n'' [[factorial]]s of [[positive integer]]s.

This is the same as their sum, with the [[parity (mathematics)|odd]]-indexed factorials multiplied by [[-1 (number)|−1]] if ''n'' is [[parity (mathematics)|even]], and the even-indexed factorials multiplied by &minus;1 if ''n'' is odd, resulting in an alternation of signs of the summands (or alternation of addition and subtraction operators, if preferred). To put it algebraically,

:<math>\operatorname{af}(n) = \sum_{i = 1}^n (-1)^{n - i}i!</math>

or with the [[recurrence relation]]

:<math>\operatorname{af}(n) = n! - \operatorname{af}(n - 1)</math>

in which af(1) = 1.

The first few alternating factorials are

:[[1 (number)|1]], 1, [[5 (number)|5]], [[19 (number)|19]], [[101 (number)|101]], 619, 4421, 35899, 326981, 3301819, 36614981, 442386619, 5784634181, 81393657019 {{OEIS|id=A005165}}

For example, the third alternating factorial is&nbsp;1!&nbsp;–&nbsp;2!&nbsp;+&nbsp;3!. The fourth alternating factorial is −1!&nbsp;+&nbsp;2!&nbsp;−&nbsp;3!&nbsp;+&nbsp;4!&nbsp;=&nbsp;19. Regardless of the [[parity (mathematics)|parity]] of ''n'', the last (''n''th) summand, ''n''!, is given a positive sign, the (''n''&nbsp;–&nbsp;1)th summand is given a negative sign, and the signs of the lower-indexed summands are alternated accordingly.

This pattern of alternation ensures the resulting sums are all positive integers. Changing the rule so that either the odd- or even-indexed summands are given negative signs (regardless of the parity of ''n'') changes the signs of the resulting sums but not their absolute values.

{{harvtxt|Živković|1999}} proved that there are only a finite number of alternating factorials that are also [[prime number]]s, since 3612703 [[divisor|divides]] af(3612702) and therefore divides af(''n'') for all ''n'' &ge; 3612702.{{sfnp|Živković|1999}} The primes are af(''n'') for
:''n'' = 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 15, 19, 41, 59, 61, 105, 160, 661, ... {{OEIS|id=A001272}}
with several higher [[probable prime]]s that have not been proven prime.
